utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to the Prosecution, to the member of the Prosecution who is in the second row. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, Stefan Waespi, Daryl Mundis and assisted by our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. There seems to be a new member too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic this afternoon, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Vedrana Residovic will be assisting me today. She is our interpreter and someone who helps us with various matters on the team. We also have our legal assistant here, Ms. Muriel Cauvin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Bourgon. Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to greet everyone on the 179th day of this case. I would like to greet the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused and all those in the courtroom and outside the courtroom who are helping us in our work. We'll continue with the hearing of our witness today. I would also like to greet the witness who is present and who had to stay overnight here as it wasn't possible to complete his examination yesterday. The Trial Chamber still needs to know or still has to decide whether we will allow the Prosecution to ask the witness questions on the basis of new documents. The Chamber deliberated about the matter yesterday, and the Chamber believes that the Prosecution pursuant to 90(H)(ii) may put its questions to the witness and may show the document under tab 6 to the witness. In this respect, the Trial Chamber would like to point out that the document mentions the subject of relations with the HVO, and this is a subject that has been addressed by the Defence when it was examining the witness because in the Defence's binder, there is a bundle of documents entitled relations with the HVO. The Chamber also notes that a document dated the 24th, 25th of May also refers to the witness and bears his signature. This is a document that the witness could comment on. The Prosecution may continue with its cross-examination. And I would also like to point out that the Prosecution said they needed another six minutes for their cross-examination. You may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Did you ever serve as 3rd Corps duty officer in 1993, particular in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was duty officer on a number of occasions or part of the duty team. I can't really say whether that was the case in May, but while I was in the corps command, I would occasionally also perform such duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did this part of your duty entail authorising reports about the daily situation on the battlefield, the relations with the HVO, and such information would be sent, then, to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was our duty to inform the superior command and submit special reports to them, and it was also our duty to draft a report. I think there was a book that we entered such records in but, yes, we did have such a duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you remember having made an entry in this book on the 24th, 25th of May, 1993, in which you informed that seven members of the 7th Mountain Brigade diffused a minefield in the Bila Valley and that the HVO reacted to this attempt by firing shells on the villages of Mehurici and Poljanice? Do you recall that incident or having made an entry about that incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, there were so many things happening at the time I can't remember that particular event. But if you have a report, if there's a written document, I could recognise my handwriting and my signature, and naturally I could comment on such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: May I ask the Trial Chamber to grant me leave to show this document to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Look at tab number 6. This is a new document which bears of ERN number, for the record, 01809764-01809767. If you please look at the first page, you find in the letterhead or the upper-left corner the dates 24th, 25th May 1993. And on the second page, on the right-hand side after the first paragraph, you find the signature. Is that your signature, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the document number 1089764, and on the following page, yes, that is my handwriting and that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you stay on the first page and on the upper right-hand side you see it is addressed to somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber has granted leave to show this document pursuant to Rule 90(H)(ii). I think one of the conditions of this rule is that my colleague establish the information he wants to verify through this witness and why such information important to the Prosecution's case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution -- could the Prosecution tell us what the purpose of this question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For the time being, I'm just trying to establish that this is indeed a report written by him and that it was forwarded to the 3rd Corps Commander. This is a preliminary question. As I said yesterday at the end of the day, later on it talks about the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade presence, and I just wanted to ask the witness whether based on that information which he entered whether he has a recollection about additional details which are maybe not mentioned here in this report. I'm in a preliminary step at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We still don't know what the importance of this information is, the information that the Prosecution wants to confirm and what the relation is with Rule 90(H)(ii). We don't see how this information might support the Prosecution's case. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is, we should not forget, a new document that has been shown to the witness. It's a document that comes from the Sarajevo collection which the Prosecution has had in their possession since 1998. So it's not a document that they couldn't have used in their case. It's one that they're using now for the first time. And it should be made clear whether the Prosecution, in asking these questions, is seeking at this stage to strengthen its case. I say seeking to do that. It may not end up doing that, but if that's what they're trying to do, in accordance with Your Honours' ruling, they cannot do that -- for that purpose. So that matter should be made clear as well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to the Trial Chamber, this should not be a means of supporting or reinforcing the Prosecution's case. 90(H), Rule 90(H) can only be used if a new document is being shown or only applied because the Prosecution has elements in its position that might cast doubt on an witness's testimony. It would have been more useful to ask the witness whether, as far as he remembered, the 7th Brigade, in May, participated in an operation. And if the witness said no, he could then be shown the document. You are proceeding too rapidly, and this is why the Defence had objections to make. Having clarified that, please proceed because the witness is in a position to comment on a document. But in future, what we follow this procedure, it would be necessary to remind the witness of what his testimony was and then confront him with the elements in your possession. You have to go stage by stage. I know that both parties want to move on rapidly, and this might have resulted in some confusion, but the Trial Chamber does understand the reason for the objections, and the Chamber also understands the Prosecution's purpose. We'll assess this matter subsequently. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution just wants to point out it's not its intention to strengthen its case why are we tendering this document into evidence. Quite the contrary, to refresh the witness's recollection about the incident and ask him for additional details he might recall or for some other explanations which he can give about the report he has written on the 24th, 25th of May, 1993. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You stated that you didn't recall that particular incident. If I may refresh your recollection by looking at your report, if you please look at page 1 and section 3, which is entitled "Relations with the HVO." And on the bottom of the B/C/S original of the first page, on the third line above the bottom there is the word "HVO," a sentence starting with the word "HVO." Can you please read out that sentence for the purposes of the record? And in the English text it's the first page, in the second line from the bottom it says "The HVO reported," there. Witness, if I may ask you to read that sentence out, please.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The HVO reported that our forces had attacked the village of Postinje, but the fact is that seven members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade set off to clear a minefield, after which the HVO fired two 82-millimetre mortar shells on the villages of Mehurici and Poljanice." End of sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Having read this after such a long time, does this in any event -- in any way refresh your recollection about the incident?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it really doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You're mentioning here that seven members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade are clearing a minefield, or in the translation which is available for everybody in the courtroom, it says they defuse a minefield. Do you understand what clearly or defusing a minefield means, and can you enlighten us on this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I wrote down is something that I believe was contained in one of the unit's reports. Right now, I couldn't say what was meant by this because I wasn't in a situation in which I could issue instructions of any kind. If this is something that was done, I have no further explanations for it. My task was to draft a report on the basis of a report from a subordinate unit, and that is what I naturally did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand this. But since you have worked in the military for such a long time, clearing or defusing a minefield, this is sort of military language. Can you explain what that means, please?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. To defuse or clear a minefield means to disable it. You can clear a minefield in a number of ways. It can be partial or complete. Well, that's all I could say, but if you require any other details, please say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My only question is: Do ordinary soldiers have the ability to clear a minefield or is there certain training necessary to clear a minefield?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was being trained, we were all trained to do this. As a rule, one doesn't use ordinary soldiers for such a task, but naturally it's very important that if you find yourself in a situation in which you have to help yourself to survive, and this concerned all soldiers at the lowest level, too, it was necessary to be sure that you could take action to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: There are three places mentioned here in the one sentence, Postinje, Mehurici and Poljanice. Do you know whether these locations are located in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that -- well, as far as Postinje is concerned, no, I don't know. Poljanice and Mehurici, I know these places. They should be in the area of the Travnik municipality, in the direction of Vlasic. That's all I could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You stated earlier that you had forwarded -- or you had served as duty team officer for -- on numerous -- or on some occasions within 1993. Here you're reporting about members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Do you remember reporting about members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in the Bila Valley in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't remember such a detail. So many things happened that it's difficult to remember. But since I did write the report -- as I have said, we wrote reports on the basis of what we received in operations centre. We received reports from all subordinate units in the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: One more last question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think there's just a mistake in the transcript. There as something missing. The witness said on page 9, line 6, that he didn't know where Postinje is. This is what I understood the witness to say and this has not been entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could the Prosecution ask the witness whether he knows where the village referred to is, because it's not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, you ever heard what the Presiding Judge has said. I could show you a map on which you could look for the location of Postinje and try to identify it, or do you recall where the village of Postinje is, whether it is in the Bila Valley or not. Let me ask this question first.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, I do not know where the village of Postinje is. If you're asking me that again, that's my answer. As far as the other two villages are concerned, I said that Mehurici is near Vlasic, and it was probably in the territory of Travnik municipality, and that's probably the case for the other village, Poljanice or whatever the name of the village was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the leave of Your Honours, a map could be shown to the witness. This is tab 7 of this binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence is on their feet. I would like to remind you, before I listen to what you have to say, that he was the duty officer in May. So perhaps he is familiar the area. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The map is not problematic, but we want to know what the Prosecution is trying to determine. What are they after? Perhaps if the Prosecution put a direct question to the witness, but if we knew what the Prosecution was seeking to establish, we might be able to save a lot of time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps it would be good to clarify something. The witness said he didn't know where Postinje was located, and my colleague wants to show him a map that any one can read, a map within which these places are marked, so I don't know what the purpose of showing him this map would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that Mr. Bourgon's comment is relevant. What is the Prosecution trying to establish, because we are running around in circles, and I personally don't see where you're trying to go, and I think that the Defence, who also wish to save time, would prefer you to put a direct question to the witness, all the more so in that you are allowed to put leading questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have twice asked the witness whether he knows where Postinje is, the location marked -- mentioned in the document, and the witness has twice responded he doesn't know, and certainly it is the aim of the Prosecution to establish the presence of 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade's members in the Bila Valley, and this map could just enlighten Your Honours that indeed the second location, Postinje, mentioned is indeed in the Bila Valley. That's all the Prosecution tries to show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the Prosecution's objective is concerned, the Prosecution wants to have confirmation of the presence of the 7th Brigade in the Bila Valley, and in particular in these three villages. What would the Defence say about that? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, whether the witness recognises the map or not, he said that he received information, a report he forwarded. We can't ask whether a unit was in a certain location or not. He said what he could say. I don't see what other information we could obtain from this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition to that, this document was shown to the witness as a new document to seek to refresh his memory. He has stated that the document doesn't remind him of any of these details and in our submission the matter should therefore be at an end. He has looked at the document and he can't say anything more about the document, having looked at it purely to refresh his memory, and in our submission no further questions therefore can be put to the witness on this topic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has deliberated and believes that the Defence of General Kubura is absolutely right when they say that the witness should not be shown the map. The Prosecution is invited to put another question instead of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. showing the map to the witness. You have very little time left, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever heard of a location called Postinje, which is located approximately one kilometre away from Maline and two kilometres away from Mehurici, Poljanice?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have heard, but I don't remember. I have just seen the map. I have spotted that place, but it really doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Neuner. And now on to the Defence. I believe that they will have some additional questions arising from the Prosecutor's question. If you have any new documents or questions that do not arise from the Prosecution's questions, then you can always ask the Chamber leave to ask such a question to avoid any confusion. Mr. Bourgon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence of General Hadzihasanovic does have a few questions to put to the witness. I would like to send the excuses of my colleague who started with the examination-in-chief of this witness yesterday, but she could not be present today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have noticed her absence, and now you have explained why she couldn't be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Husic. I have just a few questions for you arising from the cross-examination of my colleague, and the first one deals with the very last issue which was raised concerning de-mining. Now, I would like to know from you your opinion to the following situation: If you have minefield to defuse and you have no specialist to do it within your unit would it be normal to call upon another unit which is not in your territory to provide you such specialist if they have some?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. If my task was such or if I was in the middle of such a mission and encountered a situation for which I did not have a specialist on my team, then I would ask for assistance. In any case, I would try to avoid using my own men for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Husic. With respect to questions which were asked to you concerning your role as a duty officer within the 3rd Corps, I would like to know to what extent you assess the information that you receive before passing this information up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did assess information, especially urgent information. The information speaking of certain incidents which did not show the signs of developing further, we just stated them for what they -- what they were. It was not our duty to put additional make-up on what we received because this would not have been real reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you did receive, good or bad, it was passed on the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Husic, deals with the difference between the intelligence map and the map found in the office of General Hadzihasanovic, a question which was put to you by my colleague. I would like to know, would it be normal for all departments within the 3rd Corps Command to have a map on which would be plotted the information that is specific to their function? For example, artillery would have artillery-related information, engineers would have engineer-related information, logistics would have logistics-related information, and intelligence would have intelligence-related information. Is that the way it works?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. This is what it should be. I believe that my colleagues had similar maps in their offices. How much was marked on those maps it is hard to say. For example, on our intelligence map, we did not mark the positions of our reconnaissance units unless those were engaged. And I'm primarily referring to the unit that was under our direct command. As for the other level, the level below us, we did not -- we did not receive information as to where the reconnaissance units were engaged. We were not duty-bound to receive that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Husic, in response to a question by my colleague, you said that General Hadzihasanovic did not look at your intelligence map on a regular basis because he had his own map. My question is would the information on the map which was in General Hadzihasanovic's office, would that be information at the operational level if not the strategic level because that is his function?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information on the map which I can't recall would consist of the information on subordinate units. Obviously, such a map cannot contain every little detail. Those maps would usually cover bigger areas, and they would not lend themselves to a great detail. And yes, yes, this would be at the operational and strategic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Husic, how much time ahead does a corps commander have to think and to view the events?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is very difficult. In many situations, it depended on the development -- developments on the ground. And since I was never in that role and since I am still not trained or educated for that, it would be very difficult for me to provide you with an expert response to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Husic. I appreciate your candidness. Now, in response to a question by my colleague, you were talking about listening on the radio in terms of gathering information, and what I would like to know is what is the importance of having secure radio communications in wartime?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my question, Mr. Husic, is did the 3rd Corps have such means to secure its radio communications?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. As far as I know, we did not have any special device for encoding, and what we had was used together with some codes or signals. We did not have a special device that would provide you with a dedicated radio line. Those people who were trained and educated knew that this was a source of information, although there was a lack of discipline in using such devices. This was one of the advantages to, say -- when it came to the collection of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question on this topic, Mr. Husic: The fact that the resources of the 3rd Corps were lacking to secure its radio communications, would that -- did that make the 3rd Corps especially vulnerable when looking at intelligence service of the HVO gathering information on the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: During the course of the cross-examination, I haven't touched upon the technology used for intercepting radio communications as such. This could have been well covered during the examination-in-chief done by Ms. Residovic yesterday. This is certainly a new question which didn't arise out of the cross-examination, which didn't touch radio communications, devices to intercept communications. To my recollection, there wasn't a single question asked about the equipment available by the Prosecution's side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you understand the objection. You should have asked for our permission for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With all due respect for my learned friend's objection, we have asked this question because he came here to talk about that. If the Prosecution decided to ask questions for -- about the means of interception, I don't see why I should not ask the question in order to confirm their resources. But I will strike that and I will move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, maybe I have omitted to remind you that yesterday the Prosecution asked a question about the interception or the listening-in communication. The Defence says that they should be allowed this question because yesterday you asked the question about the interceptions. They should be able to ask that question. Do you remember? Do you remember that you did indeed ask the question about the interception? Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the page in front of me, but we -- I remember that a document was shown to the witness, the document that was talking about the psychological and electronic propaganda, and the -- and the witness asked from his units additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You may proceed. You can ask that question because it is in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, I will say my question once again, and it goes always follows: Considering the lack of resources within the 3rd Corps to secure its radio communications, did that make it or make the 3rd Corps especially vulnerable to the capture of information by the intelligence services of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Neuner, the question is as follows: Considering the lack of resources within the 3rd Corps to secure its radio communications, did that not make the 3rd Corps especially vulnerable to the capture of information by the HVO intelligence? What is your objection to this question which at first glance seems to be of a rather technical nature? I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: At first glance it seems to be of a technical nature but the use of the word "vulnerable" is turning this rather neutral question into a leading question. If the witness is of the opinion that this is indeed so he can state it after being asked a neutral question. This means of equipment - and again the Prosecution hasn't asked any question about it - that this is vulnerable is, in the Prosecution's opinion, a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right there. They word "vulnerable" may turn the neutral question into a leading question, but I believe that Mr. Bourgon did that to save time. Mr. Bourgon, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Let me just clarify my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Just as an add-on to my question, did the lack of resources make the 3rd Corps vulnerable more or less because of the lack of resources?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without all saying whether we were more or less vulnerable, generally speaking if you lack such means as we lacked at the time, there is a far greater possibility for your communication lines to be tapped into. And even if you -- you use certain codes or signals that could have different meanings, it is more probable that they could be used by the enemy if the enemy gets hold of the tables with all these signals. Even if you do have encryption systems and encoding systems and if you have people that do the coding, then if these people are well trained, then it is much better than if it is done by an individual. And that makes you less susceptible to intercept by the HVO. And yes, we were much more vulnerable, because we did not have any such means. We would have been less vulnerable if we had better means, and the HVO would not have had such a huge opportunity to collect data on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Husic. I'd like to move to another topic which is that of psychological propaganda. My colleague asked you many questions in relation to this form which was sent to all units to fill in and send it either on a daily basis or on a weekly basis. I would just like to know from you whether the following are examples of psychological propaganda that you would like the units to report to the corps command. The first example is the following: If the HVO knows that the armija has received orders to react only in self-defence, would the HVO, attempting to spread rumours that the ABiH as launched an attack in a village to create confusion, is that an example of psychological propaganda?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a leading question. My learned colleague may try to ask the witness what he believes what psychological propaganda may mean, but in putting such very detailed examples and abstract and hypothetical examples to the witness, my colleague is leading this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't believe that this is a leading question. The witness is the one who was in charge of the intelligence service, and he was the one who designed the form that was sent to all the units, and it served for obtaining information from the units amongst those information on propaganda. Maybe that is fear that he will mention the Mujahedin, but we just want to show the witness certain examples, three examples, and ask him whether these are the examples of what was done by the psychological propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we give you authorisation, can you give us the other two examples? You have said three, and you have just given us the first one. Can you give us the second and the third example?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The second example is the fact of spreading rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Neuner, we're going to take a stance, but we want to be very clear on the examples before we decide whether the witness may answer or not. We would like to know what Mr. Bourgon wants to ask, but before that, let's ask the witness to leave the room. Usher, can you please accompany the witness out of the courtroom, because we don't want the witness to hear what Mr. Bourgon is going to read to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The second example and the third example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly the second example: To spread rumours that a brigade of the 3rd Corps has accepted to be placed under the HVO control in order to inspire the other brigades to do the same and create a feeling of defeat. The third example: All the false rumour that may affect the morale of the soldiers of the 3rd Corps. We believe that the three examples will serve for the witness to say whether these are the examples of psychological propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall retire to deliberate. --- Break taken at 3.12 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the three questions to be put to the witness with regard to the problems of psychological propaganda, the Chamber believes that the three questions to be put can only prompt one sort of response and that it will be yes and that in that sense, the questions are leading, which is forbidden in the course of examination-in-chief or additional questions arising from the cross-examination. You cannot ask these questions because the questions are leading, and they are already suggesting a response. Mr. Usher, can you please fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed, Mr. Bourgon. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Witness, I have one last topic I would like to cover with you. This has to do with a document, a new document, which was shown to you yesterday by my colleague in relation to a meeting held by the corps commander. Do you have this document with you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the document C3, or are you referring to some other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The document, Mr. Husic, is -- bears the number, looking at the version in Bosnian, it bears the number -- no. I just have the English version here. The version in your language, yes, it is the document C3. Sorry. I had another copy here. It is the document C3. Now, my first question, Mr. Husic, is yesterday, you mentioned to my colleague that you did not recall a specific comment that was made but that you did recall attending this meeting. I would like you to turn to your contribution to this meeting. And in the English version, it is on page 7. And in Bosniak, it would be on page 01814209. Have you found your contribution to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, I would like you to read for yourself your contribution to this meeting and tell us whether you remember the specifics of the comments you made on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how much of your contribution to this meeting you remember today, 12 years later?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember this meeting. Having read what it says here, "intelligence assessment," well, this corresponds to the situation at the time. That's what I could say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Trial Chamber how many times it was possible for the corps commander to get all of his officers together for such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what is the purpose of a meeting where the corps commander gathers all of his officers together?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually one makes detailed breakdown on the situation in order to make the appropriate assessments as to what action should be taken or if there are important things that all the commanders should be informed of, and the staff by the commander. Well, these are the situations in which such things would be done, but naturally this is only possible if the situation is such that everyone can be present, and it wouldn't be possible for everyone to be present very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what would be the contribution, Mr. Husic, of the corps commander at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, he could issue certain orders or, rather, he could continue to work on matters of importance regardless of whether it was important at the level of the corps, but he could try to help certain units, perhaps. Of course, usually it's impossible to take decisions at a meeting if the subject isn't familiar to everyone, but naturally if the commander has certain information that he received from the superior command, in such cases he can inform us of that, because naturally the others have no contact outside the sort of contact that is established in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. professional terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Husic, is there a reason why General Hadzihasanovic at such a meeting also requested the presence of the staff officers from the command to be present?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course it was important to monitor what was happening in subordinate units. So, for example, at least from what I can see in the proposal that I made, this was one of the aspects of the work that I had to do. Very often intelligence officers were not working in ideal conditions, so I would usually suggest that they be relieved of certain duties so that they could pursue their work, because we had very limited staff. On the other hand, if commanders of subordinate units made certain requests that they submitted to command and these requests had to do with my work or the work of my colleagues, they were there to respond to these requests immediately or to continue reviewing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, I just have one more question for you, and relates to that type of meeting in the sense that was it the opportunity for every commander and staff officer of the corps to lay everything on the table so that we knew exactly where the corps was going at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a possibility. It was possible to provide direct information and refer to issues that were burdening either the commander or us and also to refer to the situation in units or to refer to the work that staff members were involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Husic, would there be any big secret issue that would not be raised in a meeting such as this one if it affected the corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe there were any secrets there, and in any event, this is not an appropriate way to operate. It's necessary for there to be trust in wartime when it's impossible to hide oneself. So I don't think that there were issues that could have been dealt with outside of this framework if these issues concerned everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Husic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Husic, you've been shown a document today, a document that was discussed at length yesterday and today. It's a report dated the 24th and 25th of May, 1993. You recognise this document as your own document and you signed it. You know the document in question?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a report that I drafted as the head of the duty team. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that report before you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 3, "Relations with the HVO." Have a look at the sentence that starts with the words, "The HVO reported that our forces have attacked the village of Postinje." The source of the information for your report was the HVO report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to clarify something else, the clearing of mines. Mine clearing was conducted by special units or engineer units in all armies as a rule, and that was the case in the ABiH as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In our case, the engineer unit did that. Perhaps in some other armies the units involved in this work do not form part of the engineer units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that clearing mines is not offensive action in the usual sense of the term?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the usual sense of the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This would be defensive action in a certain sense, and it would be carried out without weapons.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can carry weapons. I'm not a specialist, but in any event, one wouldn't carry weapons that would prevent you from doing your job, because it's very easy to make a mistake that could cost you your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look at this document, and my colleague suggested that they mentioned -- or that mention was made of Poljanice and Mehurici. If you read the sentence to the end.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Should I read the sentence out?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can say it. "After the HVO acted and fired two shells on the villages of Mehurici and Poljanice." That's what it says in the report?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the presence of the 7th Muslim Brigade in Mehurici and Poljanice is not mentioned in the report. All it mentions is -- what it does mention is quite different.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in the course of the day, you said that you were a duty officer in the ABiH 3rd Corps. You said that you were interested in the enemy or, rather, the forces of the Republika Srpska army and later in the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague tried to paraphrase the testimony of some witnesses who have testified before this Tribunal, and I'd like to tell you that according to our records, 13 officers have testified here from units that were in the Bila Valley, and they confirm that the 7th Muslim Brigade did not exist as an organised unit in the Bila Valley. My question is as follows: Since you were an intelligence officer in the 3rd Corps, you in fact had no knowledge about which ABiH units were deployed in the Bila Valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions, Mr. President. Just a comment on the transcript. On page 27, line 25, it doesn't say that the witness worked as an intelligence officer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned, I have a few technical questions I would like to put to you, colonel. I would like to obtain certain information. That will be the purpose of my questions. I'd like to have information about the way you worked as a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 24th of May, you were on duty according to a document we had. You were a duty officer how often in the 3rd Corps? What were the periods you were a duty officer, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, perhaps two or three times a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you were on duty, were you on duty 24 hours a day or three times? Did you have three eight-hour shifts? How was your duty organised?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a team which was on duty. The team had a head. I could also be assigned the role of the head or I could just be a member of the team. Naturally, we were present, we were physically present around the clock, but it wasn't possible to sit and work for 24 hours nonstop. So there were certain shifts in the operations, and there was a period of time during which you could rest, but if the situation was such, they'd call you to come down to the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the head of the team, we can see that on the 24th and 25th of May, you were in the head of the team. How many duty soldiers is the -- or duty officers -- how many duty soldiers is the head of the team in charge of?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think that there were three of us, perhaps four of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the report that you drafted, and you must have it before you, this written report, could you assist us and tell us whether this report was a summary of unit reports which were written or was it based on the telephone conversations that you had? Was it a summary of the telephone conversations that you had? For example, I noted that in the report you mentioned a problem that had to do with cigarettes, and this concerned the 309th Mountain Brigade. It's paragraph 2 under "Our forces." You mentioned the issue of cigarettes, and further down you said that MUP members had salaries of over 50 German marks. This information that you wrote down, was it information that you had been provided with over the phone or did you receive this information via documents that came from the units themselves? Could you clarify this, because as a Judge, I would like to know what the source of your information was.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it was the duty of units to provide written reports to the corps command. In this particular case, I couldn't say whether this information was provided in written or oral form. I did not gather this information. This unit probably provided the information, and it's far more likely that the information was provided in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my last question: Have a look at page 2 of your report. We can see your signature there, and there's another signature next to it. Could you enlighten us and tell us who the other person who signed your report is? And I'm putting this question to you because in the following pages there are other reports which have been signed a second time. One has the impression that this report was checked by your superior or is this the signature of one of your colleagues who was on duty? I don't know, but could you tell us who signed next to your signature.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, I can't be a hundred per cent sure, but I assume this might be the signature of the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Corps Command at the time, Mr. Mekic Murad. We signed the report as the operations duty officer, and later the report would be examined, and as far as I can see, the Chief of Staff would then sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chief of the Main Staff of the 3rd Corps would then read the report and sign it. Did he sign it as soon as you had drafted it or did a period of time elapse before it was signed? Because as you can see on the following day someone else was the duty officer. He drafted a report which he signed and there is a similar signature. Did the Chief of the Main Staff check the duty officer's report immediately, on the same day?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. It was our duty to take the book that we had, and usually that would be in the morning. Usually two soldiers on duty would take up their shift, but depending on the situation, they would exchange the information that was necessary to be exchanged. But when this was signed and when the reports were read, I don't know, because that was not something that I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well, are there any other questions that arise from the technical questions that I have just put to the witness who was the duty officer at the time? The Prosecution, no questions? Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, this concludes your examination. I would like to thank you for having come from so far to testify. You have answered all the questions put to you, and I would also like to thank you for having answered the technical questions I put to you about the role of the duty officer at the time. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish you a good trip home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quarter to 4.00. We'll now have our technical break, our obligatory technical break. We'll resume at about ten past 4.00. I believe we have a witness available for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We do have a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume at about ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume. I believe that the witness that is scheduled now has to leave tomorrow. I would kindly ask the Defence to stick to the time. You said is you would need an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Actually, I will be as brief as possible. It certainly will not take more than an hour, maybe even 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we are going to deal with the documents tendered through the previous witness tomorrow. We shall now have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Let me first check whether you hear the interpretation of my words in your own language. If that is the case, can you please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a Defence witness. Before you take the solemn declaration, can you please give me your first name, your last name, the date of birth and the place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am General Roderick Cordy-Simpson. I'm a retired general. I was born in England on the 29th of February, 1944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was Chief of Staff of the United Nations Protection Force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before the International Tribunal or a national court with regard to the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina or is this, rather, the first time you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have testified once before in the case of Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kindly read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you have already testified in the Kordic case. Were you a protected witness or did you testify in open court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I know that you have to leave tomorrow morning. That's why we don't want to waste any time. We want to finish your testimony this afternoon. Let me give you some information. You're going to answer the questions of the Defence. This will last about 45 minutes. The Prosecution seated on your right will conduct their cross-examination. After that, the Defence may have some additional questions to put to you. The Judges may also ask you questions at any time. You have taken the solemn declaration which means you are not to give us false testimony. This is more or less the information that I am supposed to give you before I give the floor to Mr. Bourgon who is going to start his examination-in-chief immediately. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sir Roderick. I would like to start this examination-in-chief rapidly by introducing the members of my team this afternoon. We have had the opportunity of meeting but for the transcript my name is Stephane Bourgon. I am accompanied this afternoon by Ms. Vedrana Residovic and Ms. Muriel Cauvin, and together we represent General Hadzihasanovic. Sir Roderick, I would like to begin by going over quickly your career, and I will do so by leading you through your resume with the consent of my colleague. You are a career armoured officer who spent 35 years in the British Armed Forces before retiring in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your career you have participated on numerous occasions to international missions including in Northern Ireland, Germany, Cyprus on a United Nations deployment, as well as Bosnia and Herzegovina where you deployed twice in 1992-1993, and again in 1996-1997.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct. I left at the beginning of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your career, you have commanded soldiers

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct. I left at the beginning of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your career, you have commanded soldiers at almost every level, from the tank squadron, which is the same level as an Infantry Company, to the armoured regiment, armoured brigade, and even at the armoured division level where you commanded the first United Kingdom armoured division composed of 25.000 regular force troopers.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During your career, you also occupied eye-level staff positions such as Chief of Staff northern army group, an international force; Chief of Staff British army of the Rhine, and of course Chief of Staff of UNBH command in 1993.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before you retired, you were a three-star general, to use a well-known expression, and you were deputy commander of NATO forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Finally, following this deployment you were given your knighthood by the Queen, hence your right to be called Sir Roderick, and today you are the national president of the British Veterans Association?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have just finished as the national president after four and a half years. But, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. My first question this afternoon is I would like you to explain your duties as Chief of Staff of the BH command in 1992-1993.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The headquarters was established in a fair amount of hurry, and we were given warning of it in September 1992. I was Chief of Operations at northern army group at the time, and therefore had a formed headquarters Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which I was able to use to take to Bosnia-Herzegovina when we deployed within a month. I of course had to leave over a third of my headquarters behind because they were German officers, and they were not allowed to deploy for political and national reasons. But I had a formed headquarters that allowed me to deploy fairly quickly into theatre. The role that we were given and my duties, therefore, were to assist the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Jose Maria Mendiluce from Spain and his people in distributing humanitarian aid throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in order to do that, we had to establish some form of security in the area so that the unprotected convoys of humanitarian aid could be moved freely within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can you, for the benefit of the Court, say who commanded the BH command and what was your relationship between the commander and yourself?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: General Philippe Morillon of France was my commander. General Philippe established his headquarters quite rightly in Sarajevo where he was close to the political forces that were at work at that time within Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had only a very small headquarters, and I established the main headquarters of BH command in Kiseljak, which is some 12 kilometres north of Sarajevo. It gave me a more secure environment in which to operate, as we were a headquarters and not a fighting force, but it did create obviously a problem in maintaining close communications with my commander at all times. As a result, I used to travel into Sarajevo at least three times a week so that I was able to discuss things with General Philippe Morillon, hear his views, take his orders, and then return to my own headquarters to implement the commander's requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. A quick question: What is the advantage for a commander of having a strong headquarters or command element to perform his duties?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Clearly the need to have a headquarters that reacts quickly in a situation that is as volatile as it was in Bosnia-Herzegovina is absolutely essential. Having a headquarters that can operate under such pressure is of paramount importance. I was very lucky. I had a number of officers that I knew well, a number of soldiers that I knew well from my time in northern army group who I could rely on and trust, and they could get the headquarters and implement my orders very quickly. It allowed me also to integrate the new members of the staff which came from France, Canada and Spain; in other words, the contributing nations that weren't in the northern army group. I was allowed to get them into the headquarters in a way that they quickly were able to adapt to their new responsibilities. In other words, we were able to plug into the team rather than everyone coming in from different areas trying to find out who was good, who was weak, who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would it be responsible for you to name the major players you dealt with with respect to the VRS, the HVO, and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The major players that I dealt with on a very regular basis - in other words at least once a week - would be General Gvero who was the deputy commander of the VRS, with Colonel Tolimir who was his political military advisor, Colonel Blaskic who later became General Blaskic, with Colonel Kordic representing the HVO, and Colonel Siber who represented the BiH. We knew them at that stage as the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, do you know who was the commander of the 3rd Corps at the time, and was he ever involved in meetings you attended?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Of course I know that the defendant was the commander of 3rd Corps, and I am 99 per cent certain that during my time in 1992-1993 I'd never actually met the defendant in Bosnia-Herzegovina or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it, General, what this you refer to the defendant, you mean General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I mean General Hadzihasanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, could you elaborate as to what was the focus of your work and mission in Central Bosnia in 1992-1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: My main task, as I saw it at this time as, was to ensure that we produced some form of plan that enabled the UNHCR to operate as freely as possible in the tasks that they had been given of producing humanitarian aid. My further task was to try -- and in order to achieve this, my further task would be to try and create some form of ceasefire so that we could achieve security in the area. So I was dealing very much on at one stage the political side but also very much on the senior military side of what was going on in Bosnia. I was also responsible for ensuring that Zagreb and New York were kept informed with everything that we were doing, answering a constant stream of demands, normally in the middle of the night from New York, as to what was going on, and trying to anticipate what was going to happen next. Finally, there was inevitably a huge amount of outside political demands from the contributing nations who wanted also to know exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you -- do you remember how many United Nations battalions reported to the BH command at that time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I had a British battalion, a Canadian battalion that was coming in. It had some difficulties getting into theatre because the Serbs made it quite difficult for us. I had a French battalion in Sarajevo. I had a Spanish battalion based in Mostar. Also in Sarajevo I had an Egyptian battalion and a Ukrainian battalion, and those in turn answered to commander sector Sarajevo, who was initially an Egyptian brigadier general but subsequently was a French general, and they in turn answered to me at Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. With respect to the British battalion, do you remember who was its commander at the time, and if so, what was the performance of this officer during this period?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Commander of the BritBat, as we knew it, with the 1st Battalion of the Cheshires was Lieutenant Colonel Bob Stewart. This was an armoured infantry battalion from Germany. They came into theatre slightly after I got there in October and early November 1992. They had a huge area of responsibility at the time because, as I explained, the Canadian battalion arrived a bit late because the Serbs made it very difficult to get them in, and therefore their area of responsibility was right the way from Gornji Vakuf all along the Serbian front line at Jajce, Travnik, all the way out to Tuzla and all the way up the central part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the area that we are probably going to discuss today, which was also extreme -- became extremely volatile. The battalion performed extremely well under great pressure. They took casualties. And Colonel Stewart commanded them excellently. And I would add that at the end of the tour, I was responsible for writing the citation for him that got him awarded the distinguished service order, which is about the highest award for bravery in command that our country gives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you remember any significant events involving yourself and Colonel Stewart in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. We had a major incident in Central Bosnia when there was considerable pressure and the alliance between the Bosnian forces and the HVO was beginning to fall apart. There was the road that ran through Gornji Vakuf down through Vitez and all the way past Kiseljak, Busovaca, Kiseljak and on into Sarajevo had a little village called Kacuni in it, and I think on the 25th of January, that road was cut with a roadblock. I could not allow it to remain blocked because it was essential to the UNHCR to bringing all our humanitarian aid into Central Bosnia and, furthermore, into Sarajevo. It also was essential for the whole of the United Nations troops for the freedom of movement that we needed not only to get our own supplies in, fuel, ammunition, et cetera, but in order to carry out our task. I therefore ordered Colonel Stewart to come from one side, from the north in Vitez to unblock it. And I would go from the south to unblock it so that we could meet at Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you remember yourself travelling to Kacuni checkpoint to solve this issue, and if so, why would you at your level of command or position be involved in an incident in a local area?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: First of all, we had no troops south of the roadblock. Secondly -- other than in Sarajevo, which I would not have been able to extract. Secondly it was, as I've explained, of such importance that I had to get that block -- roadblock open, and so I did. Yes, I travelled north that day in a Land Rover, and on the way we met a number of HVO checkpoints, illegal checkpoints, I would add. Some of them told me to stop and I told them I intended to go on. I was -- eventually one tried to stop me and fired at me with an AK47 which he missed. I think he was probably the worse for wear for drink at the time. And we drove on. There were a series of other roadblocks across the road of trees with mines on them, but we managed to negotiate our way around them until we got to Kacuni itself where there was a large tree lorry, a lorry that carries trees, across the bridge in Kacuni effectively totally blocking the road. I stopped there and got out. There was a bit of firing going on from around in the hills, and I met up with Colonel Stewart beside the road. His Warriors were on -- the Warrior armoured personnel carriers were on the other side of the bridge, but we met up and we had a discussion as to how we were going to get this place freed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And can you explain what happened? Did you succeed in opening up the checkpoint, and what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: We persuaded the people who were controlling the lorry that the road was not going to stay closed any longer and that I needed to get the Warriors through onto our side and that once we were through we would then come back up the road going back north towards Vitez. One of reasons for that is that the press had arrived from the north and were on the wrong side of the roadblock. But another reason I really wanted was to get the roadblock open. After some negotiations, probably of about an hour, they agreed that they would allow the roadblock to be removed and they would allow the vehicles to come back north later on. I then proceeded south with Colonel Stewart and the press vehicles that were on the wrong -- had been on the wrong side of the roadblock, and we proceeded south to a little village just north of Kiseljak called Podzivinisku [phoen], which is where the press were based. I then stopped there and told them that they had now got back to their base and were safe. I then told Colonel Stewart that he was to return north and was to make sure that he was to go to 3rd Corps and make the necessary arrangements to have a ceasefire by 6.00 the next morning and that the roadblock at Kacuni was to be lifted and he was to replace it with his own vehicles, if necessary. I would go on to Kiseljak, which was only about a half kilometre away anyway, and I would go and see Colonel Blaskic and get a ceasefire from him. I proceeded into Kiseljak and met up with Colonel Blaskic and had two meetings with him that afternoon and evening and told him that I required a ceasefire by 6.00 tomorrow morning and that I, he, and representatives of the 3rd Corps were to meet up at my headquarters in Kiseljak at 10.00 the next morning so that we could formalise a ceasefire. 3

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And the meeting you are talking about for the 26th of January, did it take place, and if so, can you describe what you recall from this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I recall it very clearly. It did take place at 10.00. Colonel Stewart arrived with Colonel Merdan, who was a deputy commander of 3 Corps. General Blaskic arrived with his political advisor and one other person who I don't recall but was there with him but didn't come into the room. I believe that Patrick Russell from the ECMM was also present at that meeting. There were of course interpreters as well. We had a fairly long meeting about a major -- all the various issues that we could, and we were making slow but nevertheless good progress towards creating the necessary trust that was needed to get a ceasefire signed. At some moment about three hours later, the third man that I referred to from the HVO contingent burst into the room that I was conducting the meeting and gave Colonel Blaskic a piece of paper which he read and said that his people were -- some of his people were being massacred at a village which name I no longer can recall and that the meeting, therefore, was -- he could not go on with the meeting any longer and that he would now have to go away and investigate this. I have to say that I clearly realised that the meeting was at an end and there was no ceasefire signed, but I was also aware that the man that had come in with the piece of paper had had no access to outside information as he was inside my headquarters, and therefore I suspected that it had been prearranged. I told Colonel Blaskic that I expected him to return the next day without fail at 10.00 and it was a matter of his duty to do so. I told Colonel Merdan that he was to go and between now and 10.00 the next morning to investigate the claims of Colonel Blaskic and report back to me the next day at 10.00 but that I intended that this meeting would go ahead without fail the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. The next meeting the following day, did it take place, and if so, can you describe the context in which this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. It took place at 10.00, as I had directed. Colonel Merdan returned with Colonel Stewart. Patrick Russell from the ECMM was also there. (redacted) (redacted), and Colonel Blaskic and his political advisor also came. In order to ensure that no more outside influence happened to my meeting ordered the Danish security guards at my headquarters that no one was to be allowed in or out of my headquarters without my authority. Over the next few hours - and I can't remember exactly how long - we painstakingly went on with the meeting towards a ceasefire. Colonel Merdan started by telling us what he had done in order to ensure that the -- to investigate what had happened the previous day, and he came in with a report that satisfied me that he had at least investigated it to the best of his ability in the very limited time that I had given him. It presumably satisfied Colonel Blaskic also, as he agreed to stay on at the meeting, and we progressed slowly but surely towards a signed ceasefire. We eventually got to the agreement and the ceasefire was signed. Almost immediately afterwards, another man appeared saying that Fojnica and Busovaca were in flames, whereupon --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry I think I need to interrupt you. I believe the Presiding Judge would like to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please have a redaction on page 45, line 9. The name of the witness is mentioned there. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, this is my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The matter is simply that some person mentioned did testify but not in open court, and we needed to remove the name of this person from the transcript. Please, can you resume describing what happened immediately following the signature of this agreement on the 27th of January?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. The -- there was a third person from the HVO delegation who immediately said that Busovaca and Fojnica were in flames. Blaskic immediately said that the agreement was off, but I held him there because I was able to prove that Fojnica was calm. It was by pure luck that a brigadier coming, a British officer, had just come from Fojnica and told me that the whole town was totally calm. In fact, it was market day. I was able to ring up the Dutch-Belgian transport company in Busovaca, who were based there, and they confirmed that Busovaca was totally calm. I was able, therefore, to say to Colonel Blaskic that his information was totally false, and at that moment I then put him with Colonel Merdan in front of the television cameras and the newspaper reporters to say that they had agreed a ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Did you obtain any further information concerning those allegations made about Fojnica and Busovaca later on?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.
