About an hour later, the Dutch rang from Busovaca to say that one house had been torched in Busovaca, but it was a Muslim house, but that it happened considerably after the person had interrupted our meeting in Kiseljak. So it was not directly connected. More importantly, I was rung up at that moment by the military assistant, I think, to Lord Owen who was in Geneva saying that Mate Boban who was the political leader of the HVO in Geneva had announced that Busovaca and Fojnica was in flames and therefore he was not proceeding with the Vance-Owen Peace Agreement in Geneva. I was able to confirm to him that it was not true and I could prove that it was not true. At the same time, the BBC told me that Serbian Belgrade Radio was reporting that Kiseljak was in flames, which they were picking up over their net, and I was able to tell them also that it was not true. It seemed to me there was a major disinformation campaign going on at this particular moment, at this critical moment in Geneva to try and persuade the world that the Bosnian forces were attacking against the HVO forces and to derail the Vance-Owen Peace Plan in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Now, do you see a link between this disinformation campaign and the actions of the HVO during the meetings of the 26th and 27th January --

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- along with the policy of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm quite convinced that Colonel Blaskic did not intend to sign an agreement and get a ceasefire in Central Bosnia. It was not in the interests of the HVO, who could see that opstinas 8 and 10 were critical to their future, and they were at that moment being discussed in Geneva. At the same time by the constant allegations of attacks in Busovaca and Fojnica, they would be felt that they would be seen by the world as the victims at the particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry, I have to repeat my question. I think you do not have to answer question, but at line -- page 47, line 25, my question was not on the transcript, and my question was whether you saw a link between the disinformation campaign, the actions of the HVO during the meetings of the 26th and 27th January and the HVO policy. I now move on to my next question, General, and I would like to know if during the meeting of the 27th January, the second meeting, whether you remember setting up some kind of a commission during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. In order to maintain -- to monitor the ceasefire that we had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. got, I set up a joint commission. I placed it under the leadership or direction of the ECMM, who were based in Busovaca. I did so because, one, they were based in Busovaca, which was the centre of where the problem was; secondly, they had excellent communications and knew the area very well. They had good radios, good equipment, good vehicles; thirdly, the British battalion was fully stretched at that time in Gornji Vakuf, along the confrontation line, in throughout their area of responsibility. I insisted that the ECMM had with them a representative of the HVO and a representative of 3rd Corps in order to give impartiality to the commission, and I ordered them to -- that their task was to investigate any complaints, go to any tension points to try and defuse them, and to be able to report back to me within three days, I think it was, by the Saturday, that they were to come back -- to report back how much they had found, how much they were able to defuse so that we would then be able to get a much more formalised agreement signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, the ceasefire negotiated on the 27th, was it respected by the parties?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Fundamentally, yes. There were a huge number of never-ending allegations of violations of it. Most of them were unfounded, and the commission was able quickly to investigate them and prove them unfounded. Some of them were almost certainly instigated by the HVO, but fundamentally the ceasefire held during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, General, deals with the meeting you -- or not the meeting but you referred to the meeting of 30 January for the commission to report. Do you know if such a meeting took place on Saturday, the 30th of January?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, it did. It took place in Vitez. I ordered Colonel Stewart to lead it and to take forward and get a more formalised agreement with both 3rd Corps and the HVO and to tidy up any details that we had obviously missed three days before and as a result of what the joint commission were reporting. I didn't do it myself because by now it was firmly down at that level, and in addition, Sarajevo was going very sour on us at this time and there was a considerable amount of fighting going on in and around Sarajevo, and certainly we lost three French troops at about that time, and I had to get my focus down there. In addition also, there was a major troop contributing nations meeting about to take place which I would have to represent BH command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, do you know if this meeting chaired by Bob Stewart, whether it led to further developments in respect of the signing of ceasefire agreements?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, it did. We then realised that we had the basis to take matters further forward, but in order to do so, we had to involve both 1st Corps as well as 3rd Corps, and since it was now at that level, we needed to give it even more publicity and strength, and General Morillon decided to chair the meeting on the 1st of February, which again took place in Vitez, and General Morillon - I remember speaking to him on his way back down again from the meeting - I know had a successful meeting there and was able to develop the way forward for these two -- for both sides in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me move on to a continue topic. I would like to know whether you are familiar with the term "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'm aware of the subject of the Mujahedin, and they were quite of lot spoken about during my time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mujahedin were actually present in Central Bosnia during your tour?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Of course there were huge allegations non-stop from the HVO and the Serbs that Mujahedin were operating in Bosnia during this period. I have no evidence that I ever saw a Mujahedin force at any stage, nor did I ever have a report from any of my subordinate commands that they had seen Mujahedin organised forces in their area of responsibility. Of course we did get reports of foreign armed individuals being seen, but most of the information we came to came from both the Serbs and the HVO to us rather than from our own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. When did you leave Bosnia in 1993, and where did you spend the next step in your career?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I left in April 1993, and I had a week's leave, and then I went straight to Vincenza in northern Italy, to the headquarters of 5 Allied Tactical Air Force, because by now the no-fly zones had been imposed by New York. The humanitarian air drops were happening, and it was essential that the NATO Air Forces had some idea what really was going on on the ground in Bosnia so that we weren't facing the potential of a blue on blue of our own forces being attacked, and to ensure that the air commanders knew exactly where the front lines were and exactly where the food drops were needed. And I therefore established a tiny liaison group for four months. And I say tiny - there were only four of us - at Vincenza with 5 ATAF.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, did you continue within those four months to monitor the events in Central Bosnia, and if so, what type of information did you gather during this period?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes -- I apologise. Yes. I was in constant touch with Sarajevo and Kiseljak. I received there daily sitreps so I knew what was happening, and I was therefore able to brief the NATO air generals what was going on on the ground from what I was receiving from Sarajevo and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during this period, General, were the Mujahedin an important issue in the information you were getting concerning the conflict in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not during this time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I understand from your resume that in 1996 you returned to Bosnia for a second tour. Can you explain which position you held at that time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I was the deputy commander of SFOR, the NATO implementation, standardisation -- sorry, Stabilisation Force. I was the deputy commander to an American four-star general, and as such I was in charge of NATO operations in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you during the period that you held this position, General, obtain any information about Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Almost none about the Mujahedin as a military force. Because under Dayton, of course, they were -- no outside forces were allowed to be inside Bosnia. I had one occasion when I was discussing the case with the Turkish brigade commander in Zenica. He said that there had been a few incidents in the summer of training camps for children up in the hills which disturbed him as they were being conducted by what he described as Muslim fundamentalists. He had said that he was very keen to disrupt them and to get rid of them. And since he was a man that I had great faith in as a military man and himself was a Muslim, I assumed, therefore, that it was therefore quite a small operation on which he was very much on top of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned the Turkish brigade, if I look at page 52, line 21. Can you explain what a Turkish brigade was doing in Zenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. We -- I think we had 35 different battalions in theatre under command at that time, one of which was a Turkish -- quite small, but a Turkish brigade. It was responsible for a fairly large area of operational responsibility in Central Bosnia, answerable through MND north at that time; in other words, the American division to us in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So am I right in saying, General, this was a United Nations brigade?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No, it was not a United Nations brigade. It was a NATO brigade under command of a NATO command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, I just have a few more questions for you. Are you familiar with a document called milinfosum or military information summary?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see such documents in 1993 and while -- and if so, what did you do with this document?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. Each battalion produced its milinfosum daily into headquarters in Kiseljak. My staff would look at them. They would produce a summary which I would see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And may I ask, General, what is your assessment of the reliability of the information you found in milinfosums in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I think you've got to understand from the start that the United Nations is a totally unbiased organisation that has -- takes no side in an operation. As such, the gathering of military intelligence is an anthema to it, and it is not allowed to have intelligence-gathering capabilities, certainly not at that time in 1992. Therefore, we were not in the game of actively producing military intelligence. Therefore, we would produce milinfosums which would report anything that was given or heard or seen by anyone, much of it purely reported speech. It helped building up the overall picture of what was going on in theatre, but it was information. It was not intelligence. And I must emphasise it was not intelligence because it had not been corroborated in any way whatsoever. It was, therefore, of limited value as a document, and it was up to my military judgement as to how much emphasis I put on what was in the milinfosums or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the -- based on your experience, do you believe that the HVO was aware that there was no real intelligence gathering going on in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I think all three sides were well aware that we were not in the active game of intelligence gathering. They therefore, all three of them, used our position to feed us with as much information as they could, knowing that it would probably appear in the milinfosums and some of it would stick and some of it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, do you see a difference between the situation report or the exceptional assessments produced by BH command in 1993 and mil information summaries?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. The situation report was a factual document. The one that went out from BH command each day would be signed by myself and would go to Zagreb and would go to New York and was therefore very carefully produced and would hopefully only have real military information in it. The military information summaries were there to try and aid us in building up an overall picture of what was going on in theatre but was not confirmed fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned at the beginning the issue of Sarajevo and especially that at some point things were getting sour in Sarajevo. Can you explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what the situation was in Sarajevo at the time and the impact on this situation on the conflict as a whole?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. It -- Sarajevo was the focal point of everything that was going on, as far as the world was concerned, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The fighting was normally fairly intense. I can hardly remember many days when there was not sniping, shootings of some form or other going on in Sarajevo. The roads were regularly cut, the airport was regularly shelled, and everyone was looking at Sarajevo. Whether that was what was intended we probably failed to understand at the time, because while the Serbs were attacking Sarajevo, the world's press and everyone else was not looking elsewhere, at some of the ethnic cleansing and attacking that was going on in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. While everyone was focused on Sarajevo, probably some people were not watching with much care what was going on in certain other parts of Central Bosnia, in Gornji Vakuf and the likes, Turbe, Travnik, Tuzla, et cetera, all of which were suffering pretty badly. I believe in retrospect, and I failed to see it at the time, that it was probably to many people's advantage to keep the eyes of the world on Sarajevo. Certainly to the Serbs it was. Probably to the Croats it was because it didn't directly affect them, and to a lesser extent in some ways I believe it also was to the BiH as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I only have two more questions, and the first one is could you provide your opinion on the situation in which the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina 3rd Corps in Central Bosnia, what situation it was in and especially the challenge faced by its commander due to the situation?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, they were a new corps of various disparate units facing an enormous challenge. The first challenge of course was a major attack from the north by the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, all down from Travnik, Turbe, Jajce, all that area there. The second challenge they faced was that they were, of course, isolated in Central Bosnia. The Serbs had interior lines of communication back to Belgrade to keep -- to Serbia to keep themselves resupplied. The HVO also had interior lines of communication to keep themselves resupplied from Croatia with food, people, weapons, et cetera. The 3rd Corps had no such advantages. In fact, they had every disadvantage. They were cut off. Food, ammunition, weapons once used or lost could not be replaced. Therefore, in every way they had a major military disadvantage over the other two factions involved in this conflict. In addition, unlike my headquarters who arrived on the ground trained, people knowing each other, they had no such advantage having not had a proper corps before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What kind of challenge would that place, General, on the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I would suggest to you it placed an enormous challenge on him and one that I certainly wouldn't have like to have placed on my shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question is one that deals based on your substantial command experience. I would like to know, General, if you see a difference between the responsibilities of a battalion commander and the responsibilities of a corps commander towards soldiers and how much of a personal involvement do each of those have.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. It is my belief that battalion command is the last time an officer will directly influence how his soldiers perform on the battlefield. He is responsible. He is the man they see, and he can will them to fight better than any other person in the battalion. Once you become a brigade commander or a divisional commander or a corps commander, that direct influence is lost. As a brigade commander you tell your battalion commanders what you require them to do, but you cannot permanently influence the individual soldiers within that battalion to fight harder, fight better, or anything else. Certainly when you become a divisional commander, you have totally lost that ability to influence the battle of how people fight, and as a corps commander, you are way above that. You are directing the battle at the high tactical, I would put it, level, but you are not directly influencing how soldiers fight on the ground at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your view, General, what should a corps commander do to prevent violations from happening, bearing in mind what you just said as to what he can and cannot do?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: He can only lay down to his battalion commanders, or in the case of a corps commander to his divisional commanders and his brigade commanders, how he wishes operations to be conducted and on what sort of code of behaviour. Having passed that information, he must either expect that his subordinates will carry out his orders, or if he finds subsequent that they haven't carried out his orders, then he must order an investigation into why that has not happened. But he cannot influence the individual actions of soldiers on the ground at a particular moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have one last question and one name that did come up during your testimony is that of Blaskic. Could you provide your assessment concerning Blaskic, and I would like you -- to refer you to a specific incident which is commonly known as the potato incident.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic and myself knew each other very well. I met him regularly at the Mixed Military Working Group. I met him regularly in and around Kiseljak, and I respected him as a hard and tough soldier. He clearly had a political agenda around this period in January 1993, and I've referred to that throughout. The potato incident is possibly slightly amusing. Sometime in early 1993, Blaskic came to see me and he said, "I have" -- I can't remember if it was three or four lorry loads of potatoes which he needed taking to his people in Busovaca, which were starving, and he was worried that the BiH forces would intercept his trucks and steal the potatoes and would I give a UN Protection Force to see it through to Busovaca. He persuaded me that his people in Busovaca were starving and that I had to get this convoy through. I somewhat reluctantly agreed because it was not my job to effectively take food through for the warring factions. At the last minute I ordered my headquarters staff to transfer all of the potatoes from Colonel Blaskic's lorries onto UN lorries. In doing so, we found a large number of hand grenades, quite a number of RPG 7 anti-tank rocket launchers, and a vast quantity of small arms ammunition in amongst the potatoes. I was all for naming and shaming Colonel Blaskic for the incident, but my commander General Morillon, being more subtle than I was, decided that we would not name and shame him, but we would [Realtime transcript read in error "hit"] let him know very clearly that we knew what he had done and that if he stepped out of line again we would not be so lenient with him, and that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to Mr. Kubura's Defence team. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions at this time for the witness. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. There's an error in the transcript. On page 59, line 15. The witness said -- I don't believe that that was General Morillon's intention or General Cordy-Simpson's intention. I don't think it was the intention to hit Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Look, General, at page 59 that is at line 15 and it says "decided that we would not name and shame him but we would..."

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yeah. There's something wrong there. Be more subtle than I was. Decided that we would not name and shame him but we would let him know very clearly that we knew what he had done and if he stepped out of line again we would not be so lenient with him. And that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll give the floor to the Prosecution now. Then I should point out that we'll be having our technical break at 5.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. I would just like to go over a few Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. points you discussed with my learned colleague Bourgon, and I will be referring a couple of times to your testimony in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just for your reference, Mr. President, the witness testified in the Kordic case on 4th of August, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just on the last issue about Colonel Blaskic at that time, I believe you testified in Kordic that you generally trusted Blaskic except for that one occasion being the potato incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. That is fundamentally correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And another quote from the Kordic case, you were asked the following question: "On a more general level, did you find in your five months in Central Bosnia that it was routine for fanciful claims to be made on the part of each one of the three competent ethnic factions?" Probably component ethnic factions. And your answer was: "Without any doubt, yes. Exaggeration was all part of the game for propaganda reasons." Would that be a fair assessment of your opinion at that time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go into the Mujahedin issue, and I would like to start with an incident which took place very, very early on in your detail in Bosnia. Do you remember that on the 29th of October, Colonel Blaskic had informed General Morillon - and I paraphrase the information - that there was growing infiltration of Mujahedin mercenaries posing as journalists on diplomatic passports saying that there were some 3.000 to 4.000 of them having joined Muslim fighters and being protected by diplomatic immunity? Do you remember that? I believe you were also asked in Kordic about that incident.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The answer is, yes, I do remember the [Realtime transcript read in error: "ak case"] accusation. I was not with General Morillon on that particular day because that was also the day that Jajce fell and I was further north. But, yes, I remember saying it and the transcript coming from Morillon's forward headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe in the Kordic case when presented with the Morillon report, you said: "It was a constant theme of the Croat delegation," and you continued, and then you said: "There was clearly some evidence that there were some Muslim fighters from Arabic countries in Bosnia, although I have to say the figure of up to 4.000 was probably -- we had little evidence to bear such a high figure out." And that's in your Kordic transcript at pages 6197 to 98. Would that still be your evidence today somewhat later than in 1999 when you testified in Kordic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. Remember I did say there was some evidence of Muslim fighters from Arabic countries, evidence, although no figure to bear out such a high figure as that. I would repeat that seeing individual fighters around does not, in my opinion, point to the fact that there are large foreign bodies of Mujahedin in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a document, in fact it's a Defence exhibit, and I believe it originates from BH command. It dates 7th January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would like perhaps first to give you the proposed exhibits for this witness. And the document I would like to show to the witness is tab 8. And that will be for the record DH0545, 7th January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: While the documents are being handed out, I just thought as there's a break, if a clarification to the transcript could be made, Your Honour. That's at page 61, line 18. It's recorded, the answer: "Yes, I do remember the ak case," in the English transcript. In fact, the witness said: "I do remember the accusation." That's the accusation being made about the numbers of Mujahedin. If that could just be corrected for the transcript. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I take it you are familiar with this document, at least the format, and I believe it even says information within the -- COS I take it that's Chief of Staff. So you would have been privy to this information; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to find out what page you're referring to at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. It's tab 8.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. I've got the page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you see info it says COS, Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I guess that would be you?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in just the bottom of this document under B.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It says: "Locals in the BH area report snipers of Middle Eastern origin in Bosanska Krupa. These individuals did not speak Serbo-Croatian." And then comment: "The presence of Mujahedin from the Middle East has been properly reported. These are seen as interlopers and have even been reported to have fought with the local Muslims in the Bihac pocket." Do you remember this specific message from BH command, a daily information summary of 7th January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The answer is, now that I've seen it, yes, but I'm going to have to add that I was not in theatre on the 7th of January. I was trying to get back to Sarajevo, and I was stuck in Zagreb. I didn't get back because I know the date exactly because the assassination of the deputy Prime Minister was now the focus of all my attentions. I don't in any way deny the responsibility, but I was not actually in Bosnia at that time, but I would have seen this document as back reading on my return, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And so before we heard about Colonel Blaskic reporting something about Mujahedin, here we have a UN UNPROFOR document reporting similar information about the presence of Mujahedin from the Middle East. So that would be, in fact, the information you told me colleague you were lacking information generated from your own kitchen, if I can put it as such.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It's a comment, and actually it's not a comment that would have passed my signature at the time had I been the Chief of Staff present at the time, because again it is a comment, and I feel that -- and I don't believe that there is sufficient evidence to have made such a strong statement as has been written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to the next tab. That's tab 9. And this appears to be a different format, yet I believe you were the releasing officer.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It states 17 January 1993. The subject: "Special assessment waiting to return to Geneva." And it sort of ties in what you said in examination-in-chief about the linkage perhaps between Geneva, Mate Boban, the other players and what is happening in the ground in Bosnia. And in the first paragraph you indeed talk about this proposed plan, Vance Owen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document for the record is DH0590, a Defence exhibit, tab 9 in this bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm interested in now, General, in the second paragraph. There you say, assuming that you drafted it, the perhaps development or whatever: "In the negotiations is paralleled by the relative lull in combat between Serbs and the allied parties across the country. However, tensions brought on by the uncertainty related to the proposed settlement are exacerbating factional problems between the HVO and the principally Muslim elements of the Presidency forces." Now, assuming that you wrote it or perhaps you remember the thought process, what is meant by "principally Muslim elements of the Presidency forces"? And perhaps if you can tell us first again - I believe you said it already - who are the Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: In those days, we used to refer to the BiH as the Presidency forces. The reason that it was done is that at my level in negotiations, Colonel Siber would come from the Presidency in Sarajevo, and at that stage the BiH command preferred to have themselves called, particularly in Sarajevo, the Presidency forces. Subsequently, it became the BiH forces. I don't personally read anything very significant into it but that -- if I had put down the Bosniak forces or the BiH forces or the Presidency forces, I was certainly not trying to make any significant point that I can see. I would though emphasise that a large -- I have no idea of the size but quite a number of people that were fighting in the Presidency forces were not Muslims. There were certainly a number of Croats, Colonel Siber being one, and he was the Chief of Staff of those forces in Sarajevo, and I am sure that there were others. In fact, I know there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So by principally Muslim elements, these would be distinct from the general mix of Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: This would, at that stage being referred to -- up to that stage, we had had a semi-joint command of forces fighting the Serb forces. Here we were beginning to see the clear signs of a break-up in that fragile alliance and, therefore, I have said the principally Muslim elements. In other words, one was seeing the break-up of what had been a loose alliance as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But the break-up occurring between the HVO and the Muslim army or within the Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. I believe -- what I'm referring to there is the break-up between -- a clear delineation between the HVO forces and their partners, their semi-alliance forces from the principally Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But just turning again to this the principally Muslim elements of the Presidency forces. I -- you know, it's very difficult for you to go back and even for me to second-guess what you have meant, but does that suggest that within the Presidency forces there were principally Muslim elements which contributed to the exacerbation of problems?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I think I know where you're coming from. At that stage, I can promise you I did not mean any fundamentally Muslim forces inside the ABiH. I -- if I had wanted to, I would have said so, most categorically. If that is where you want me -- you're trying to get me to say, I categorically will state now that I was not meaning in any form some form of fundamentalist Muslim forces within the BiH force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, then, what do you mean by principally Muslim elements? That means just all the Muslims taken away, the Croats and perhaps Serbs who were fighting within the ABiH? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I was saying that BiH forces being principally a Muslim force, they and their Croat loose allies up to then were breaking apart at this stage. That is all I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me show you a document which has been discussed with a previous witness, and that's in your bundle, the tab number 11. That's a milinfosum dated 29th. Now, you told us that you has -- have seen summaries of milinfosums and perhaps you may recall the -- this document. It's number 11, tab 11 of this bundle. Its a 1st Cheshire milinfosum dated 29th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I see, Mr. President, that's a new document, in fact. I don't intend to go into that. I thought it was the one we had discussed before, Mr. President, and that will be tab number 7. So I'm not going to rely on this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Tab 7. That's P944. That's again a milinfosum. I take it you recall the format now --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry. This is also a new document although it does have a P number. I'm sorry to interrupt my learned friend. It was only introduced in respect of a previous witness, Colonel Stewart in respect of refreshing his memory. So in my submission my learned friend has to establish that there's a basis for showing this document to this witness. In addition to that, if he's going to show the witness the paragraph about the 7th Brigade, this is a matter that was not raised at all in examination-in-chief, and he would require Your Honours' leave in order to address that as a separate and new topic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness could be directed not to go into the document at this point, please. I'm happy, Mr. President, to ask a preliminary question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Put questions to the witness to refresh his memory. General, don't have a look at the document. You should look at the member of the Prosecution who will be putting his question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: General, do you recall having seen either a milinfosum or a summary, as you told us today, of a milinfosum coming from the 1st Cheshire Battalion command commanded by Colonel Stewart dated the 27th of January, 1993, which talks about a specific battalion which in -- within the 7th Muslimanski Brigade that consisted, amongst others, of at most 100 to 150 external Mujahedin from Islamic countries? Do you recall having seen such a summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: In my submission, my learned friend does have to ask for your leave if he is going to address this topic because it was not addressed at all in examination-in-chief. The 7th Brigade or any of the brigades within the 3rd Corps were -- were not the subject of the examination of this witness. Indeed this witness was way beyond what was happening at the brigade level. As Your Honours know, Colonel Stewart himself was not even engaged at that level and he was the subordinate of this witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I could respond, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On that question of the Prosecution it's true that the Defence counsel did not mention of the issue of the 7th Brigade. So if you immediately start referring to the 7th Brigade, you should state the purpose of putting this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, I was surprised myself that the witness started to talk about Mujahedin, because the 65 ter summary of this witness doesn't mention anything in relation to that. But then the -- my learned counsel asked him about any information of Mujahedin, and the witness said that there was a lot of talk about that, that the warring factions were making complaints, but he himself wasn't appraised of any sort of hard information. And he also said that he received summaries of milinfosums. So I take it he would have been interested in any hard information coming from the British battalion about these Mujahedin. So I think it's probable that by reading the milinfosum it will refresh his memory. And let me state another point, Mr. President, Rule 90(H)(i) says: "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief." He talked about Mujahedin. Second, credibility of the witness; I don't think that's an issue at this point. And third: "Where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party for the subject matter of that case." And he clearly, Mr. President, can talk about the Mujahedin as he has proved already. And that's obviously part of the Prosecution case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what the Defence seems to be objecting to is the following: The witness did mention the Mujahedin but you're establishing a link immediately between the 7th Brigade and the Mujahedin. You're moving on to the 7th Brigade directly, but it would be appropriate to show the witness the relevant documents and ask him whether among all the documents he had, the milinfosums, et cetera, whether there was any reference to the matter. It's necessary to prepare, to put this question to the witness, because you've moved on to the 7th Brigade immediately, and you established a link between the Mujahedin and the 7th Brigade, and this is the reason for which Defence counsel raised an objection. Do you understand what the Defence is objecting to? But perhaps Mr. Dixon could tell us. Mr. Dixon. We will then have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Your Honour. My learned friend started reading immediately from the document which mentions the 7th Brigade and that's why I objected. The witness was not asked any questions about that brigade. And perhaps if my learned friend is to proceed any further, that is the first question that must be asked, whether he knows anything at all about that brigade, and if he doesn't, given the level that he was operating at, it's of course for the witness to answer that in some detail, then we can proceed from there. If he knows nothing further, then in my submission no further questions should be asked about this matter. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can respond to the objection and we will then have our break. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The only point is the witness talked about Mujahedin, and this document talks about Mujahedin bringing it into some organised fashion being part of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I think the witness testified he has not seen any evidence that the -- if I can quote him directly: "No -- No evidence of any Muslim Mujahedin force, organised forces." So that would suggest otherwise, and perhaps seeing it might refresh the memory of the witness. And again, he testified he has seen summaries. So it would surprise me that such an interesting information would have escaped his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's quarter to 6.00 now, and we will resume at about five past 6.00 or ten past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will render our decision, now. But Mr. Bourgon, is there another issue you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's the same problem. I wanted to say something about what the witness said with regard to these documents. The witness said [In English] They would produce a summary which I would see. [Interpretation] The witness never said that he had seen the milinfosum, so I believe that this is important information, given that the Trial Chamber will be rendering its decision on the matter. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What would the Prosecution have to say about the comments just made by Defence counsel, before we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. render our decision, since as we said we will be rendering our decision about allowing you to refresh the witness's memory by using the document. So what would the Prosecution have to say in response to Mr. Bourgon's comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, I have full faith in the witness's independent opinion. It's just a little dangerous, you know, if we sort of make these arguments in front of the witness, but I'll do it anyway. This document is not evidence, and we are not proposing to have it put into evidence. It's really merely to refresh the witness, this recollection. Perhaps he has heard it and that's our point of view. And we don't seek to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber deliberated on this issue during the break, and we accepted the possibility of the Prosecution refreshing the witness's memory by showing the document but only if the witness had previously been asked so-called -- well, had previously been asked questions to refresh the witness's memory. And it's only if the witness is still not quite clear that you can refresh the witness's memory. So there are two stages. Before refreshing the witness's memory, you should ask the witness your question, because if the witness can answer your question it's not necessary to show the witness the document in question. You should first ask the witness your question, and if the witness is still not able to remember, you may then show the witness the document to see whether this might refresh his memory, because as everyone knows, the witness is testifying about events that took place over ten years ago, and it's quite possible that he has forgotten certain things. I'll give you the floor now. First put your questions to the witness, and you can then show the witness the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you reviewed the summaries of these milinfosums, do you remember having read a summary which discusses the role of the Mujahedin within the 7th Muslimanski Brigade? Do you recall that? And I'm talking about the end of January 1993, specifically 27th of January.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I regret I don't now 12 years ago remember reading that milinfosum. I -- as I said in earlier testimony, I tended not to read each battalion's milinfosum. I tended more to read their sitreps, and of course I then was responsible for producing the BH command sitrep and occasional assessments, but no, I regret that I do not remember seeing a milinfosum from a battalion on the 29th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 27th of January.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I apologise. 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No problem. Do you think it would refresh your memory if you see this two-page milinfosum about this subject of whether indeed you have seen it and perhaps incorporate it into the daily BH command sitrep? Do you think it might help to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I'm quite prepared to look at it, and it may refresh my memory, but it's, as I say, a long time ago. And as I also said, I tended not look at the battalion milinfosums as they tended to be at a level that my staff dealt with rather than myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you think the information about presence of the Mujahedin in that area would have been important information which you would have been interested in at that time?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. Except that if there was a firm intelligence of Mujahedin, then I would expect it to have been brought to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I would like to show the witness this exhibit with the purpose of refreshing his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could now look at tab 7. That's this 1 Cheshire milinfosum number 88 dated 17th January, 1993. And the paragraph I'm interested in is on the second page, the second paragraph. And if you could just read through it yourself, because it's been discussed here before and read out. And perhaps you can tell us whether you have anything to say about the information contained in here.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I don't recall having seen it. I probably should have done. You -- as it is clearly an important element. However, you must recall that on the 27th, 28th, 29th, as I have already explained in my testimony, I was dealing with some fairly major incidences, some fairly important conferences and trying to get a ceasefire in the Central Bosnia under control. And also, I was dealing down into Sarajevo where there was some quite unpleasant businesses going on. I don't recall having seen it. An oversight, but probably an oversight on my behalf or my staff's behalf in the fact that they didn't bring it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move on to the next exhibit, Mr. President, and this is Defence Exhibit DH0664. And unfortunately I have not prepared it as part of my bundle because the Defence had announced it would use it but had not used any exhibits. And my all-knowing case manager just tells me that this specific document is tab 10 of the binder. Tab 10, DH0664.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This, General, appears to be minutes of the meeting of 27th of January 1993, which you chaired, and you see that in paragraph 1, attendees. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, first of all, in paragraph 4 it recalls that Colonel Blaskic referred to yesterday meaning the meeting of the 26th about the assassination of an HVO delegation, apparently the incident that was mentioned the day before. Do you remember anything about this assassination of an HVO delegation being discussed?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not being discussed. But this was referring to the piece of paper that had been handed to Blaskic the night before when he stopped the meeting and walked away from it and said to me, Some people have been murdered in a village, which I don't recall the name. That is the assassination of which he is now referring to here as recorded by Patrick Russell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could it be that this village was called Dusina?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I haven't a clue, I am afraid, it's so long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in the second page as well. Here after paragraph 6, and I believe it's probably paragraph 7, it reads as follows: "The chairman then asked both sides whether they were able to control the forces under their," I take it their command, "and whether they both wanted peace. Both sides answered both questions positively." Do you remember that issue being discussed?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have absolutely no reason to believe that I didn't say that. It would have been precisely what I would have said to them to ensure that if they left the room having agreed a ceasefire they could implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there any mentioning of any forces, you know, they had not control over and which needed to be contacted in order that the ceasefire be implemented?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. They said that they would implement the ceasefire and would go ahead and were able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we are finished with this document. Going back to a quote from Kordic, your Kordic testimony, again on the same subject. You were asked about, you know, Kordic and Blaskic as you were today, and you were asked about your conclusions about their control over the HVO in Central Bosnia. And you said, and I quote you: "It was quite clear that they had signed at that meeting. They were able to -- what they had signed at that meeting they were able to deliver insofar as the fighting died down. And although we had isolated incidents of burning of houses and shootings, the large-scale attacks that had been going on prior to this ceased. Therefore, my conclusions were that Kordic and Blaskic between them were able to exercise the necessary influence over the military forces in Central Bosnia as was the 1st and the 3rd Corps Commanders of the ABiH over their forces." Pages 6220 to 21. Do you stand by that also today?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to the next document, and this is now DH0648. And while that's being distributed to everybody, I can ask you the author of this document is a person, and we have heard evidence before, Ambassador Beaussou or Beaussou. I believe he arrived in the scene in January and he was an ECMM person. Do you remember having met this person or do you know anything about him? Perhaps you can look at his name. He appears on the second page as printed. Colonel Stewart testified his name was Beaussou with an S at the end, so I'm not sure which one is the correct spelling. An ECMM officer. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I vaguely remember him and nothing more than vaguely do remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, this document which he authors dates 25th of January, 1993, roughly a week after your assessment which we have discussed before the break. Now perhaps you can tell us something about a comment he makes. And this shows up on paragraph 3 on the first page towards the bottom, and I quote: "The dangers for the whole area are obvious for the outcome of the Geneva talks, for the fate of the populations, as well as for the possible interference of Islamist forces encouraged by the victimisation of the Muslim community." Now, do you something about the possible interference of Islamist forces in this process you were about to embark or complete?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know what he based that evidence. I mean, that is his assessment. It's not mine, and it's the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Let me continue with a slightly different subject. You touched upon and said that: "The BritBat troops, the battalion, performed extremely well under great pressure."

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe Mr. Stewart in his book said, and I quote him: "In my view, the soldiers I led in Bosnia are the best in the world." That's page 211 of his book. I believe you have read his book.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that that would -- you would agree with his assessment?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart would be bound to say that, wouldn't he. I'm sure a French colonel would say the same about his battalion or a Swiss commanding officer would say the same about his. They were very good, and that is all I will say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, let me take it a little bit further. Where was the -- being curious now and I'm sure the Trial Chamber is as well having seen the commanding officer here. Where were the weaknesses, if anything? Was it the officers? Was it the soldiers? Was it the equipment? Can you tell us a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Of course there was some weaknesses in the battalion. They were pitched into a very, very serious situation at very short notice, and of course mistakes were made. I don't think it's for me at this stage to name individual weaknesses within the battalion, nor do I think that it does any good. Of course there were times when I personally had words with Colonel Stewart and corrected him on where I thought things needed correcting. That was my job. No individual battalion is without a fault. It is inevitable under such situation that people get tired. They make mistakes. Just before the incidents of which we are talking, a young soldier in the Cheshires battalion was killed by a sniper. These tensions, particularly for a battalion that has never seen war before, and young soldiers, has an effect. I think at that 1st Battalion Cheshires did extreme well under very trying conditions. All battalions in theatre and all units in theatre make mistakes. I don't think the Cheshires made very many.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I accept that. Let me just ask something very specific. Did Colonel Stewart in the contacts you had with him or perhaps he vis-a-vis General Morillon or when the Prime Minister came to visit you, did he ever complain about, for instance, that he had not enough intelligence or he wasn't satisfied with the way his intelligence or gathering -- information-gathering unit was operating? Did he ever raise the issue with you, that he needed to have it staffed up or anything? Do you recall anything?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I don't recall it as an incident -- as an issue that he raised directly with me. I think it would be fair to say that I was asked whether I require additional intelligence-gathering forces at one stage by the British and said that while I remained a United Nations force, I would not have them in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was, by the way, the person in charge of receiving all the information coming from the different battalions, milinfosums, sitreps, direct contacts with the commanders and so on, with your BH staff?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: The chief mil information officer in the BH command headquarters was a French colonel, Colonel Constantini.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me - and I believe I have about two or three subjects more to cover - briefly touch upon a command issue that you talked about at the end of your chief. You were asked and you responded about the challenge the corps commander was faced with and the difficulties, and you also talked about the different levels, corps, brigade, battalion. I believe there was a discussion about delegating something to the battalions. Now, let me just ask you, and you have experience, an enormous experience, obviously, and you have seen different commanders of different countries, let me ask you about that and especially the word "delegation" sort of made me little wonder. I just want to see where we are. I have a quote from a British General, I'm sure you know him, General Francis Richard Dannatt. He had testified in another case in the Tribunal, also a case which concerned a corps commander. And let me read out - it's very brief - what he said: "I have to say that because I go back, Your Honour, to one of my earlier points of yesterday that command is a personal thing, and the commander must take and does take personal responsibility for all that goes on in his zone of responsibility." Do you agree with General Richard Dannatt on this point?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course I agree with him. He was well taught. He was one of my brigade commanders when I commanded a division. But being serious, what he has said there is absolutely correct, but it doesn't say that he is responsible for every incident and every single thing that happens in his enormous sphere of command. Of course things will go wrong. It is the subsequent action that a commander takes when things have gone wrong that is a test of whether he is a good commander or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I said that I would add that of course he needs to know, he needs to put on notice of what's happening. It's no strict liability when we talk about his responsibility. Do you agree with me? He needs to be put on notice of what's happening.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: If you're saying to me he needs to be informed when things are -- have gone wrong, yes, I agree. That is absolutely correct. He cannot possibly know under such a large sphere of command what every individual soldier is doing at every minute of the day. If he did, he would not be a very good commander. He would be too much down, as we say, in the weeds and not up doing his proper job as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But nobody takes away his personal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not at all. But his personal responsibility at this stage, though, if something has gone wrong is how he reacts to how it has gone wrong and not try and shift the blame somewhere else but to investigate it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to the meetings, the sequence of two or three meetings on the 26th and the 27th of January, and I want to show you a couple of documents. But let me ask you first. You testified that the meeting, the first one on the 26th of January which you had sort of requested or initiated, it started at 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you are certain about that?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Incidentally, you talked about this Kacuni incident, the checkpoint, and you mentioned I think the lorry across the road. You mentioned HVO. You didn't mention ABiH. Just to make it clear, that checkpoint which cut the road between Kiseljak and the Lasva Valley, that was an ABiH checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. It was amongst a row of HVO checkpoints leading up to Kacuni, and then actually across the bridge in Kacuni was an ABiH vehicle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, there's been some issue about this piece of information which Colonel Blaskic relayed to you and indeed the participants during that first meeting, and you stated in your witness statement of 1995, in your Kordic evidence, and today again that Blaskic's allegations were sort of unfounded because you went and checked with an UNMO, and he reported back that Busovaca was quiet.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I said that I checked with the UN Transport Battalion, which was a Dutch-Belgian battalion based in Busovaca, and I checked with them on the satellite phone and they informed me that Busovaca was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that was that was on the first day, the 26th, or the second, or on the both days?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That was on the second day which I presume was -- I can't remember now but I think it was the 27th meeting. The first day failed, the first meeting failed because of the assassination, in inverted commas, when Blaskic and Merdan left. On the second day it was reported that Busovaca was and Fojnica was in flames. I checked with the battalion in Busovaca, which was a Dutch-Belgian battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So on the first day you did not check the information that was relayed by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. I ordered Colonel Merdan from the 3rd Corps to investigate Blaskic's allegations and to report back to me at 10.00 the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he came back and said yes, there indeed was combat operations in Dusina and that there were casualties on both sides?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I can't remember what he said exactly, but whatever he did say, he had investigated that they were presumably combat casualties and whatever he said was sufficient to keep Blaskic at the meeting and therefore satisfied him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me briefly show an exhibit, and this is in tab 3 of your bundle, and that's an ABiH press release, Prosecution Exhibit 132. It dates 26th of January, and it is 1545 hours. Just the first sentence of this public announcement: "The suffering the Muslim people in the territory of the Busovaca municipality continues," and then it goes on. So would you agree with me that even the ABiH at this time agrees that something is happening in the Busovaca area, at least on that day, on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if we can go on to the next document, and that is a document, tab 4. That's Prosecution Exhibit 133. Now, that date's the 27th of January, 1993, and it is signed by -- or for Commander Enver Hadzihasanovic. It's an evening report, and I would like you to look at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the second page. It talks about, just the last, penultimate paragraph, chronology of events around Busovaca. And it starts: "At 0830 hours, the villages of Gornja Visnjica and Dusina was shelled." And it goes on and it says at the end of the paragraph: "The terrain around Lasva has been cleared of HVO soldiers." Now, just for your information these villages of Gornja Visnjica and Dusina are about four to six kilometres north-east of Busovaca. Perhaps you recall that. Now, doesn't that suggest that indeed only the 27th there was some action going on in the Busovaca area specifically in the Dusina area? And that's not HVO propaganda. It's by the commander of the corps. I'm interested because you told us that you thought the information received from Colonel Blaskic was a major disinformation, and perhaps, you know, you haven't seen these documents, I take it, at that time, but perhaps that suggests otherwise.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I accept the fact that it suggests otherwise. I'm just trying to work out the time. 8.30 in the morning seems to -- if that is correct, well, so be it. I have no reports on it, nor did I ever see this document, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Let me ask you, just to finish up a couple of other points, I believe in late January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a clarification, please. With regard to the document that has just been shown to the witness, on page 85, line 2, the number is wrong. The document is dated 27 January 1993, P525. Can you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm much obliged, Mr. President. P525 and not P133.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In late January, probably after these ceasefire negotiations, there appears to have occurred a two-day seminar in Kiseljak when General Morillon wanted to talk to his commanders, subordinate commanders and discuss, you know, a unified approach to the problem. That's what Colonel Stewart wrote in his book. Do you remember that two-day seminar?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. One day was in Kiseljak and the second day was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe each commander had to brief, you know, his subordinate commander. First of all, let me ask you, were you present?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you remember what Colonel Stewart told General Morillon? He said in his book it was very brief, perhaps five minutes. Do you recall anything of what he reported?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I can't remember. We had all the battalion commanders in. They gave a situation report of what was going on in their area, really for the benefit of the others. We also -- it had -- I think on the second day in Sarajevo we had a press reporter to come and brief us what he saw and what he understood we were doing right in his eyes and what we were doing wrong in his eyes. I can't remember much more about it. But during that seminar, of course, life was also -- I was being called out fairly regularly for dealing with a number of incidents that were going on, not least complaints from one side or the other of violations of the ceasefire. But I do remember the seminar, yes, but I can't remember everything that was spoken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I appreciate your answers, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've eaten up my time, and I'm over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have a few questions for you. I will try and be as quick as I can because I see time is running out. My first question, General, is in response to a question by my colleague, you confirmed that in the Kordic case you mentioned that complaints by all sides was part of the game and it was part of the propaganda. If I would ask you to compare complaints made by HVO with complaints made by the 3rd Corps, how would the two compare in terms of whether -- the number of complaints and whether they were founded or not?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: There was no question that in the period that we're talking about there were more complaints from the HVO than the 3rd Corps, and I think that would be fair throughout the whole of my period there of between the HVO and the BiH, but it wouldn't mean that we didn't get a number of complaints from the BiH as we did from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as to the results of those complaints once you had verified them, is there anything you can say about the HVO complaints?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: At this particular period, the majority of the complaints I couldn't substantiate. That did not actually mean that they weren't true, but it did mean that I could not substantiate them. Either I didn't have the troops on the ground, or by the time we got to the area to try and substantiate it, things had gone cold or had got totally confused. I think one has to understand what an incredibly confused and difficult operation this was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My colleague referred you to a conversation between General Morillon and Colonel Blaskic where the issue of Mujahedin was brought up. Now, without showing you the result of this discussion, if in this paragraph Colonel Blaskic did not mention where these Mujahedins were going and that they were not going to the area of the 3rd Corps, would that also -- would you also confirm that basically this was just a complaint and you had nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes. It was a complaint and I certainly did nothing about it. And also, if I remember correctly, if was very early on, something like the 29th of October. In which case, I was on the ground, General Morillon was on the ground, but there were no troops on the ground. The troops didn't start arriving, i.e., the combat troops didn't start arriving until early November. And the British battalion was not chopped to under command, BH command, until the 14th of November. I may be wrong just on that date but it was about then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned in responding to that question that there was something about Jajce, the fall of Jajce took place on the same day that General Blaskic made this comment on the 29th of October. Do you see a link between those two events?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Possibly. I had no way of trying to verify it because I had no troops on the ground. Colonel Stewart was on the ground, but he didn't have a battalion on the ground, and it is he who told me that Jajce was falling and alerted me to the fact, and I actually went out to watch the HVO pulling back. I haven't actually ever in my mind linked the two together, but it is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to refer I to document number 8 which was discussed by my colleague, which is a daily information summary. Now, you mentioned in examination-in-chief, and this is at page 54, line 7 to 15: "We produced military information which would report anything that was given or heard or seen by anyone. Much of it was purely -- sorry, is purely reported speech. They are of limited value as a document. It was information. It was not intelligence because it had not been corroborated in any way whatsoever. It was, therefore, of limited value as a document." This document at number 8, information summary, does this document fall in the category of documents you were referring to? This is DH0545.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Not strictly in the way that a battalion -- this would be the best information that we could gather and would make comment on, but you will see that it says these reports have not been substantiated. For instance, at paragraph 2, "Local and media information only are our source." In other words, always being careful to point out that this information was not hard intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I refer you to the same paragraph that my colleague referred you to. First page, paragraph 1, where it talks about something about Mujahedin fighting with local Muslim in the Bihac pocket. Which corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in Bihac to your recollection, and would that information -- from which battalion, from which of your battalions would this information come from?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I have some difficulty in recalling, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I can be more precise. Was Bihac in the area of 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was. But I can't see who was reporting this information to us from BH command at that stage. I have a feeling it was a Danish battalion who were up in the Krajina, but I'm afraid now I have difficulty in recollecting 12 years ago who would have reported that to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, would you be able to locate Bihac on a map, and is it possible that Bihac was located away from the area of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I mean, Zenica is here and Bihac is right up there. I mean -- and I wouldn't know the areas or their boundaries at all at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to refer you to document number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with regard to this document, as we promised yesterday, we have obtained the integral text of the paragraphs which are very difficult to read, and I'm going to present to the witness the paragraphs 5 and 11. If these could be placed on the ELMO and after that I'm going to put my questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to refer you to the document used by my colleague and first to paragraph 5 of this document. And you now have the paragraph 5 in full. I would just like to ask you to look at this paragraph and if this corresponds to the report given by Colonel Merdan that you were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, this is document 0664, DH.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you confirm, General, whether this is report given by Merdan that you were referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: In broad terms, yes, I do recall. That is the sort of language - I'm not saying those were his exact words - that he gave to us at Kiseljak on the second day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Moving on to paragraph 11, which you also have, I would just like you to confirm that this is what you were referring to a little earlier when talking about creating the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no objection for him to confirm that, but I didn't talk about the commission, so if he goes any further, I would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm just asking for the confirmation that this is the paragraph that the witness has made reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, to the page before at paragraph 9. Sorry. There was no answer for the previous question, General. Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And is paragraph 9 what you were talking about about the HVO trying to again break those negotiations when Blaskic told you, as you said, that the agreement was off?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you provide additional reasons, General, why on both occasions you were of the view, regardless of the information that was shown to you, that this was theatre on the part of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: It was all part of what was going on in Central Bosnia and what was going on in Geneva at the time.
