I was quite convinced that the HVO did not want to sign a ceasefire and they did want to derail Geneva at that time. They wanted to appear the victims at that time. There may have been some elements of truth in what Blaskic was saying at the time, but it was all too much produced at the second for theatrical-type performance to be plausible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, my colleague showed you two documents showing that there was indeed some activities in the Lasva Valley which would correspond to the allegations made by Blaskic. My question to you is: Did Colonel Merdan, when he made his report, try to say that nothing had happened or did he say that combat did take place but that there was no crime?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: No. He accepted the fact that there had been fighting, and that was his position. But he had done his best in his opinion to investigate the sort of fighting that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to remind again we don't have a chance to cross-examine. If these questions would be put in a non-leading fashion like after the meeting did Colonel Merdan talk to you, what did he talk to you. You know, if he's presented with a multiple choice like he was here, it's just leading and that's unfair to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have two more questions before I finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, my colleague asked a question of you concerning personal responsibility of a commander. Now, I just would like to confirm with you that when you say that a corps commander is personally responsible for everything, who is included in the everything in terms of people?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Ultimately the commander is responsible for everything that goes on within his command. What I was trying to say was that as a commander, you cannot personally oversee the actions of every one of your subordinates, but you are responsible when they do not perform correctly to ensure that the matter is subsequently investigated and, if necessary, those who have perpetrated something are punished. That is the fundamental on which military discipline is based.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how far does that go beyond subordinates, General? If it does, of course.

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Well, if I think -- the question I think you're leading me -- or you're asking me is if someone above us -- the lowest level has been responsible, then clearly if a company commander has failed to take the necessary action, he must be punished. If a battalion commander has allowed something to happen which he was fully aware was wrong, then he is responsible and the punishment must go there. If a brigade commander, clearly it -- he must be found responsible. But the point I still was trying to make is the higher you get up in command, all you can do is lay down clear instructions. And if they are not correctly carried out, then you must investigate why they were not correctly carried out. If it's then found that your orders were imprecise or bad, then you must be responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The -- what further to your last answer do you expect the corps commander to do about crimes committed by people who are not his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, that's the ultimate issue in this case, whether they are subordinates or not under command and control, and I'm quite sure that the Defence will have an expert who will talk about his issue. But this witness has -- you would need to put all the evidence to him from the Defence, from us. We say they were under the command and control. Defence says no. It's unfair to this witness. Just, you know, let's assume they were not under control to have him giving an assessment. I think he said in theory, given his practical experience, what he can do, but I think any further would be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that my colleague has not understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Judges have understood. Your question was a general question. The Defence's question was a general question that has nothing to do with this particular case. The Defence asks the general, who has 30 years' experience in various positions and who is at a high level and who is able to answer this question. General, you have heard the questions by the Defence. Can you answer this question, the question that has been put to you? This question, mind you, is a general question. We Judges need that answer, because we are not military experts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give me one second just to read back the original question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, perhaps you can answer the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] I will ask the question again. You were mentioning in your response to my previous question that the commander must, whoever the subordinate is, company commander, higher or lower, I'm asking you what do you expect a corps commander to do for crimes committed by people who are not his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question clearly. I think it depends entirely whether he has any influence on that particular organisation which accordingly is not part of his subordinates. All he can do is report the matter higher, that there is some force that is behaving outside control in his area. He has no ability because he has no command function over someone who is not under his command. It is a fundamental military principle and one that we, certainly wherever I have been, you have to establish exactly your command relationships with everyone in your area. And I don't want to confuse people, but there is a huge difference in being opcon, operational control, and opcom, operational command. And for me it would be one the first things that I would establish, whether forces in my area were opcom to me or not. Now, that's easy because I come from an organisation that has been brought up under Staff College trainings and all the rest of. It isn't quite so easy in the confused situation that we are talking about in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't believe that if a force is operating which is not under your operational command there is much you can do when they get out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am conscious of the time but there are a few questions that I need to ask arising from the cross-examination of the Prosecution. I will be no more than three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: General, at the outset I didn't ask you about command and operational matters at the brigade level. The Prosecution has asked you to address this matter. So can you please confirm that during your time in Central Bosnia you had no dealings at the brigade level with either of the parties involved in the conflict, the Bosnian army or the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. I did not have any dealing at brigade level or, for that matter, with the Bosnian Serb army either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: So is it correct then that you had no dealings with the command of the 7th Brigade of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: I had no dealings with the command of the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And that the issue of this brigade never arose in any of your dealings while you were performing your duties in Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You were shown a military information summary of 27 January 1993 by the Prosecution. It's a new document that's marked P944. Can you confirm that the allegation contained in it that you were shown about the Mujahedin falls within the typical kinds of information and allegations that you described in general that are contained in military information summaries in that it is a reported speech, that it comes from an unidentified source, that it is uncollaborated and not based on any evidence or intelligence? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, before the witness answers, I believe the witness said - and that wasn't argued by Defence - that he had nothing to do with it, that he knew nothing about that, and he only read summaries. So it would not be fair now to have the witness, you know, comment about this compound question. I don't think he's familiar with it as far as he told us, so how can he now talk about the reliability of a source of something he's not aware of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you have heard the question. The Prosecution has the right to object, and they say that as the Chief of Staff at the time, what can you tell us? How can you clarify this issue to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will accept the fact that it says a normally reliable source in this document, but that I must repeat is not intelligence. That is information, and therefore I must make a judgement, we all must make judgements as to whether it is reliable and how reliable, and in this case, since there was no collateral evidence, I would probably have -- if I had even seen it, I would have noted it, but I would not have taken it as being hard intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I merely ask the question because the Prosecution had shown this document to the witness after some extensive discussion about whether it should be shown to him in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Only a few more questions, General. Can you confirm that the bulk of the allegations and information about the Mujahedin came from the HVO and the Serb armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: You said in your evidence in chief that you had no evidence of any organised formations of Mujahedin forces in Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you had no evidence of any organised groups of Mujahedin within any of the brigades of the 3rd Corps? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RODERICK CORDY-SIMPSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we would like to thank you for coming to testify here in The Hague. Your testimony is hereby finished. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, we wish you a happy journey back home. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is late. I'm going to ask the Defence the witness scheduled for tomorrow is he available?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now adjourn. I would like to thank everybody. I would like to apologise to the interpreters to have kept them 15 minutes longer but that is the only way we could do it. I invite everybody to come back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of February, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.16 p.m.,
